stem: What is the dot product of [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6]?
explanation_after: Dot product: multiply each pair and sum. (1×4)+(2×5)+(3×6) = 4+10+18 = 32. It gives one scalar measuring similarity. Every attention score, every recommendation engine, is built on dot products.

stem: Word embeddings represent words as vectors. The classic result 'king - man + woman ≈ queen' works because:

options.text: Computers memorised these relationships from a dictionary
Vector arithmetic captures semantic relationships: the gender direction is consistent across related pairs
Random chance — it only works for royalty words
The words have similar letter counts

explanation_after: In embedding space, queen - king ≈ woman - man (same gender direction). This vector arithmetic on word meanings is why embeddings are so powerful for NLP.

stem: At a basic level, what is a vector?

options.text: A list or array of numbers

explanation_after: A vector is a list (or array) of numbers. A 768-dimensional embedding vector (like in BERT) is a list of 768 numbers.

stem: What is the magnitude (L2 norm) of the vector [3, 4]?
explanation_after: The L2 norm (Euclidean length) is the square root of the sum of squares: √(3²+4²) = √(9+16) = √25 = 5. Vector norms are used to measure embedding magnitude and to normalise vectors before comparing them.

Vector addition is element-wise: add corresponding components. [2+1, -1+3, 4+(-2)] = [3, 2, 2]. This is exactly how gradient updates work: new_weights = weights + (-learning_rate × gradient), an element-wise vector addition.

stem: In gradient descent, the gradient of the loss function is a vector. Why does the algorithm update weights by moving in the OPPOSITE direction of the gradient vector?

options.text: Because the gradient vector points in the direction of steepest increase of the loss, so moving opposite decreases the loss fastest
Because vectors can only be subtracted, never added
Because the gradient vector is always negative
Because moving in the gradient's own direction would leave the loss unchanged

explanation_after: The gradient of a function at a point is a vector pointing in the direction of steepest increase. Since training wants to minimise loss, weights are updated as w_new = w_old − learning_rate × gradient — stepping opposite to the gradient vector, the direction of steepest decrease. This single vector fact is the mechanical core of how every neural network learns.
